description: StarFire is a one-woman mission control: one AI researcher, plenty of curiosity and an ambitious plan to make NASA’s microgravity fire research easier to explore 🚀🔥.
summary:
Do you know the exact flammability risk of materials used across space stations? If not, don't worry, navigating NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository with over 100 microgravity combustion investigations can be overwhelming, unless you already know exactly where to look.

That's why I built StarFire, an interactive assistant that turns raw curiosity into structured research discovery. Rather than presenting another passive catalog, it invites users to ask their own questions in plain English, whether about material flammability, flame spread, smoke detection, or fire suppression, and instantly serves up a ranked shortlist of relevant investigations.

Each result comes with a tailored, AI-generated research note explaining its direct connection to your question, highlighting useful metadata evidence, offering a cautious interpretation and suggesting a concrete next research step. Users can inspect the raw metadata, follow original NASA source links, compare investigations side-by-side and download a research brief. All you need to bring is curiosity and an initial query and StarFire kickstarts your research journey!

Ultimately, finding relevant research does not mean a dataset is immediately ready for modeling or that a safety conclusion is proven. StarFire keeps source evidence transparent and separate from AI interpretations, giving researchers a reliable launchpad without replacing scientific judgment. Happy researching 🚀!
details:
What StarFire Does

StarFire helps users explore NASA’s microgravity combustion investigations through natural-language research questions. A user can ask about material flammability, airflow, smoke detection, or fire suppression and receive a ranked shortlist of potentially relevant investigations.

For each investigation, the app automatically generates a question-specific research note covering:

  • Its connection to the question.
  • Useful evidence documented in the metadata.
  • A cautious interpretation of that evidence.
  • One concrete next research step.

Users can inspect original metadata, open source links, compare investigations and export a CSV shortlist or TXT research brief.

How It Works and Tools Used

I developed StarFire in Python using Streamlit for the interface, pandas for data handling, and sentence-transformers and scikit-learn for the retrieval workflow. Investigation records are collected using Playwright and BeautifulSoup and stored in a local CSV catalog.

Research notes are generated locally using HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Hugging Face Transformers, and PyTorch. The app runs locally using Apple’s MPS acceleration when available. I used VS Code for development and GitHub for version control.

Benefits and Intended Impact

StarFire aims to make NASA’s research easier to navigate, particularly for students and researchers approaching an unfamiliar investigation catalog. It connects discovery with practical follow-up: users leave with relevant investigation candidates, accessible source evidence and suggestions for what to inspect next.

Creative Approach

Instead of providing the same summary for every reader, StarFire interprets each investigation in relation to the user’s question. It combines retrieval, locally generated explanations, evidence inspection and a downloadable research brief in one workflow.

Design Considerations and Limitations

I prioritized clarity, traceability, and keeping scientific evidence separate from AI interpretation. The interface avoids safety scores and does not treat relevance as proof of dataset suitability. The prompt instructs the model to distinguish objectives, hypotheses, methods and reported findings.

StarFire remains a working prototype. Generated notes can contain errors, retrieval quality needs formal evaluation, and experimental files must be inspected before making modeling claims. It supports research discovery and not operational fire-safety decisions or scientific judgment.

Use of Artificial Intelligence / Declaration

  • Core App Architecture: An open-weights small language model (SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct) and sentence embeddings (sentence-transformers) run locally within the prototype to generate research notes and rank investigation relevance.
  • Development Assistance: I used Perplexity as an interactive assistant for code debugging, reviewing Streamlit layout choices and refining documentation clarity. All system architecture, data scraping, prompt constraints and final code decisions were authored and verified by me.
